title: Hello, Cargo! Rust's build tool
summary: You will create, check, build and run a project with Cargo, and know what every file it creates is for.

sections: PR ch1 Rust makes collaboration easier

blocks.md: After this lesson you will manage a Rust project the way almost every Rust programmer does: with **Cargo**. Calling `rustc` by hand is fine for one file, but real programs have many files and use code written by other people. Cargo handles all of that with a handful of commands that are the same on Windows, macOS and Linux.

blocks.title: A kitchen manager
blocks.md: If `rustc` is the cook, Cargo is the kitchen manager. It knows where the recipes are kept, orders ingredients from suppliers (other people's code, called **dependencies**), tells the cook what to make, and keeps the finished dishes on the right shelf. You talk to the manager; the manager talks to the cook.

blocks.title: Creating a project
blocks.md:
`cargo new hello_cargo` creates a folder named `hello_cargo` with a ready-made project inside. It also starts a **Git** repository (Git tracks changes to your files) unless you are already inside one.

Inside you will find two things: a `Cargo.toml` file and a `src` folder holding `main.rs`. Cargo has even written Hello, world! into `main.rs` for you.

blocks.explain: This file uses **TOML**, a simple settings format. `[package]` starts a section about your project: its `name`, its `version`, and the Rust **edition** it is written for. An edition is a snapshot of language conventions (2015, 2018, 2021, 2024); old code keeps compiling while new projects get the newest idioms. `[dependencies]` is where you will list other people's packages. In Rust a package of code is called a **crate**.

blocks.title: Build, run and check
blocks.md:
`cargo build` compiles the project and puts the executable in `target/debug/`. The first build also creates `Cargo.lock`, which records the exact versions of every dependency so the build can be repeated exactly. You never edit `Cargo.lock` by hand.

`cargo run` builds (only if something changed) and runs in one step, so it is what you will type most. `cargo check` only checks that the code compiles, without producing an executable. It is much faster than a build, so many Rustaceans run it constantly while writing code.

steps.title: cargo build
steps.md: Compiles the project. The word **dev** means a development build: compiled quickly, not optimized.
steps.code:
$ cargo build
   Compiling hello_cargo v0.1.0 (/projects/hello_cargo)
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 2.85s

steps.title: cargo run, nothing changed
steps.md: No `Compiling` line: Cargo noticed the source did not change and just ran the existing executable.
steps.code:
$ cargo run
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.02s
     Running `target/debug/hello_cargo`
Hello, world!

steps.title: cargo run, after an edit
steps.md: You changed `main.rs`, so Cargo rebuilds first, then runs.
steps.code:
$ cargo run
   Compiling hello_cargo v0.1.0 (/projects/hello_cargo)
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.33s
     Running `target/debug/hello_cargo`
Hello, world!

steps.title: cargo check
steps.md: Only checks for errors. No executable is written, which is why it is fast.
steps.code:
$ cargo check
    Checking hello_cargo v0.1.0 (/projects/hello_cargo)
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.32s

blocks.title: Building for release
blocks.md: When your program is ready for real users, run `cargo build --release`. It turns on **optimizations**, so the program runs faster, but the build takes longer. The result goes to `target/release/` instead of `target/debug/`. That is why there are two **profiles**: one for quick rebuilds while you work, one for the fastest possible final program. If you ever measure how fast your code is, always measure the release build.

blocks.md: Day to day you need three commands: `cargo new` to start, `cargo check` while you write, `cargo run` to try it.

blocks.title: Working on someone else's project
blocks.md: Because Cargo's layout is the same everywhere, getting any Rust project running looks like this: `git clone <address>`, `cd` into the folder, `cargo build`. If you started a project without Cargo, move the code into `src/` and run `cargo init` to create the `Cargo.toml`.

cards.back: The project's settings file: name, version, edition, dependencies.
Records the exact versions of all dependencies. Managed by Cargo, never edited by hand.
A package of Rust code: your project, or a library you depend on.
Checks that the code compiles without producing an executable. Fast.
Where development builds and optimized `--release` builds are written.
A snapshot of Rust's language conventions (2015, 2018, 2021, 2024) chosen in `Cargo.toml`.

blocks.title: Your first Cargo project
blocks.goal: Create a Cargo project on your own computer, change what it prints, and build it in both profiles.
blocks.behavior:
1. Run `cargo new hello_cargo` and `cd hello_cargo`.
2. Open `src/main.rs` and change the message to `Hello, Cargo!`.
3. Run `cargo check`, then `cargo run`.
4. Run `cargo build --release` and run the optimized program directly from `target/release/`.
checklist: The second `cargo run` (with no changes) did not print a `Compiling` line.
`cargo build --release` created an executable in `target/release/` that prints the same text.
hints: If `cargo` is not found, open a new terminal after installing Rust.
blocks.solution_explain: Cargo only rebuilds when a source file changes, which is why the second `cargo run` skips the `Compiling` line. The release build lives in a different folder, so both executables exist side by side.

questions.q: You are halfway through writing a function and want to know whether it compiles, as quickly as possible. Which command?
hints: You do not need an executable yet.
questions.explanation: `cargo check` only checks the code, skipping the slow step of producing an executable. `cargo build --release` is the slowest option of all because it also optimizes.

questions.q: In which folder does `cargo build --release` put the executable? (format: `folder/subfolder`)
questions.explanation: Release builds go to `target/release/`, development builds to `target/debug/`, so both can exist at the same time.

questions.q: Which file should you **never** edit by hand?
hints: One file is written by Cargo to record exact dependency versions.
questions.explanation: `Cargo.lock` is managed by Cargo. You *do* edit `Cargo.toml`, for example to add dependencies; Cargo then updates `Cargo.lock` itself.

points: Cargo is Rust's build tool and package manager; its commands are the same on every operating system.
`cargo new` creates `Cargo.toml` (settings) and `src/main.rs` (code); `Cargo.lock` appears on the first build.
`cargo check` is the fast compile check, `cargo run` builds and runs, `cargo build --release` makes the optimized program.
Development builds go to `target/debug/`, release builds to `target/release/`.

terms.def: Rust's build system and package manager. It builds code, downloads dependencies and runs tests.
A package of Rust code. Your project is a crate; libraries you use are crates too.
A crate that your project uses, listed under `[dependencies]` in `Cargo.toml`.
The project settings file written in TOML: package name, version, edition and dependencies.
A file that records the exact versions of all dependencies so builds can be repeated. Managed by Cargo.
A set of language conventions (2015, 2018, 2021, 2024) a crate opts into in `Cargo.toml`.
The build settings used by `cargo build --release`: slower to compile, faster to run.
